newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin to focus on debt - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin to focus on debt - newspaper.

text.p: The recently re-elected Liberal government plans to focus on reducing its debt once the country's budget deficit is eliminated, Finance Minister Paul Martin said, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported on Tuesday.
But Martin, reappointed finance minister last week, told the newspaper that his government also plans to spend in critical areas to spur growth.
He also told the Globe that the federal government does not plan on running large annual surpluses.

"As long as you are piling up debt -- which is what the deficit is about -- you have to focus on the elimination of the deficit by reducing spending," Martin told the Globe in a phone interview from Montreal on Monday.

"Once you have stopped adding to the debt, then it is clear the growth side of the equation becomes far more important in reducing the debt ratio," he told the newspaper. ""But we have to make sure that what we're investing in are the things that are going to create jobs and growth."
Canada's deficit has shrunk quickly in recent years under Martin's care, from a once-huge C$42 billion (US$30.3 billion) in 1993 to an estimated C$15 billion (US$10.8 billion) in the latest year.
The final figures for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1997, will not be released until the autumn.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien has said the country's books will be in balance within two years.
Canada's debt is expected to total C$610.3 billion (US$441 billion) in 1997-98, or about 73.1 percent of gross domestic product, one of the highest ratios in the industrialized world.
Martin told the Globe and Mail that his government is committed to reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio to well below 60 percent within a few years, but he would not set a precise target.
"We need to get ourselves on a steady, downward track," he told the newspaper. "But I don't believe that long-term targets work."

Martin and Chretien have been under pressure to loosen the purse strings after their Liberal party won a slim electoral victory on June 2. The party won 155 out of 301 seats in the House of Commons, giving left-leaning backbenchers within the party more leverage.
